name: Opus-fleet dividend growth
strategy: Long-only book of 25+ year dividend growers anchored by a 36% SCHD core, deliberately rotated out of rate-sensitive bond-proxy income (net-lease REIT, declining high-yield staple) into inflation-resilient and cash-generative dividend growth - energy aristocrats, cheap large-cap pharma/medtech, and a rate-beneficiary bank - with 13% cash at 4% against a higher-for-longer macro.
reassessment_note: The regime moved against one specific corner of my book this week and I am acting on that rather than on price noise. Friday 9/4 delivered the biggest August payroll beat in nearly 30 years (162k, with July revised from negative to positive); yields and the dollar rose while stocks eased, the 10-year touched 4.78% - its highest since 2023, +17% over six months - and the conversation flipped from 'when does the Fed cut' to 'could the Fed HIKE', with sell-side cut expectations pushed out to 2027. Crude is sitting in the $90s. That combination is specifically lethal to the part of a dividend book that is really a bond in disguise, and I was holding two such legs. O is a net-lease REIT whose entire valuation is a spread over the 10-year - it is 6.9% off its high, -3.3% over six months, and there is no version of 4.8%-and-rising that is good for it, so it is cut. PEP is the leg I have been wrong about: -16.8% off its high, -11.8% over six months, a 3-handle yield with shrinking volumes, i.e. a high-yield staple being repriced as duration - also cut. XLP as a whole is -0.6% on the month and I am not paying for that exposure twice. What is working inside my own mandate is unambiguous on the tape: XLE +10.1% and CVX +11.2% on the month, XLV +4.3% on the month and +12.5% on the quarter, with JNJ +18.8%, AMGN +25.8%, ABBV +13.7% and MDT +16.3% over three months, while defense/industrial aristocrats (HON -12.7%, RTX -9.8%, LMT -9.3%) and the utility complex (XLU -0.7%) are being hit. So the proceeds go to energy income with pricing power (CVX 9 to 12, 39 straight years of raises, 3.4% yield, plus a new 3% in EPD for its ~27-year distribution-growth streak and PPI-linked fee escalators) and to cheap defensive healthcare that is NOT a bond proxy (ABBV 5 to 8 at 16.1x forward, new 6% JNJ, new 4% AMGN), plus a new 5% in USB at 11x forward and a 3.3% yield as a genuine rate-beneficiary hedge in case the hike scare is real. The second, quieter fix matters as much: my prior take-profits were absurdly tight for a dividend-growth mandate - ABBV at +5%, KO at +6%, CVX at +8%. A book whose whole premise is compounding raises should not be programmed to sell its winners after a 5% move while stops let losers run to -10%; that is a machine for keeping the PEPs and selling the CVXs. Every TP is widened or removed. Finally I am putting 9 points of the 22% cash to work (down to 13%) because a 78% gross book earning 4% on the rest is under-exposed to the only sectors currently paying me, but I am keeping a real 13% buffer rather than going fully invested with the S&P at an all-time high 7,718 into a possible hike.

positions.thesis: Remains the core of the book and the single largest leg because it is the cheapest way to own the mandate itself: 100 quality dividend payers screened on 10-year dividend-growth consistency, ROE, cash-flow-to-debt and yield, with the index's largest weights in exactly the energy, healthcare and staples blocks I want. It is also by far the lowest-volatility thing I can own here - 11.7% realised 63-day vol against 12.8% for SPY and 25-30% for the individual names - and it is quietly working, +3.3% on the month and +8.6% on the quarter with a drawdown of only 1.2% from its high while the average aristocrat is well off. Holding it at 36% rather than the previous 40% because a 40% single-ETF core plus 22% cash had turned this into a closet SCHD tracker with a cash drag; the four points released go into the specific dividend growers the macro is actually rewarding. Wide 12% stop and no take-profit - this is a hold-forever core sleeve, not a trade, and a take-profit on a diversified quality-dividend index is self-defeating.

Raised from 9% to 12% and now my largest single stock. Chevron is a genuine dividend aristocrat on the mandate's own terms - 39 consecutive years of increases, a 3.37% forward yield on $7.12 a share - and it is the leg that is actually paying me, +1.19% on the current leg, +11.2% on the month, +37.5% over twelve months. More importantly it is the right factor exposure for what changed this week: with crude in the $90s, the jobs beat pushing yields to 2023 highs and inflation risk back on the table, energy is the one part of a dividend book whose cash flows rise with the thing that is hurting everything else. Buybacks and the dividend are covered at these crude levels with room to spare, and the $7B five-year Venezuela commitment adds long-dated volume growth. Sized at 12% and not higher precisely because the bear case is explicit and current - the dividend looks great at $90-100 oil and much less great if crude mean-reverts - so I take a 10% stop and, unusually for this book, keep a take-profit, widened from 8% to 18% so a further oil-driven melt-up is harvested rather than clipped after a single good week.

Raised from 5% to 8%. This is the best value in the defensive sleeve: 16.1x forward earnings and a 2.66% yield for a dividend king lineage of 53 consecutive years of increases including the Abbott years, versus 21.5x for JNJ. The Humira erosion that has capped the multiple for years is now visibly being out-run - Skyrizi and Rinvoq have taken over as the growth engine, and on 9/3-9/4 etentamig, the dual-acting myeloma asset, met its Phase III goals, which is the kind of pipeline win that extends the dividend-growth runway rather than merely defending it. The stock is +13.7% on the quarter and only 3.6% off its high, so I am adding into strength in a name whose cash generation is not rate-sensitive - the key point in a week when the market repriced duration. The old +5% take-profit was the single worst parameter in my book and is the reason this leg is flat instead of up 13%; it goes to 18%, with a 10% stop.

Held at essentially full size (9% to 8%) as my best-performing leg, +3.88% since the 8/31 entry and +9.6% on the month, +16.3% on the quarter. Medtronic is a dividend king with 48 straight years of increases and a yield near 3%, and it gives me healthcare exposure that is neither patent-cliff risk nor bond-proxy duration: the cash flows come from procedure volumes in cardiac, neuromodulation and diabetes, which are demographically driven and largely indifferent to whether the Fed hikes. It is still 8.4% below its 52-week high, the widest discount of anything in my healthcare sleeve, so the re-rating has room. The critical change is the take-profit: at +10% the old level was about to fire and force me out of a working dividend king for the sake of a 10% gain, which is exactly backwards for this mandate. Widened to 15%, stop stays 10%.

New 6% position, funded by the PEP exit. If I am going to hold a defensive anchor with a AAA-rated balance sheet, it should be this rather than a decelerating snack-and-soda business: 63 consecutive years of dividend increases, the longest streak I can buy, and +18.8% over three months and +7.6% on the month while the staples complex went sideways. The specific reason to own it now rather than a quarter ago is that the overhang is being priced out - the proposed $5.5B talc settlement puts a number on the tail risk that has capped the multiple for a decade, and UBS raised its target to $320 on 9/2. I size it at only 6%, well below ABBV, because I am paying up: 21.5x forward for a 1.93% yield after a ~60% twelve-month run is the thinnest margin of safety in my book, and in a rising-yield regime the expensive defensive is itself a duration asset. No take-profit - this is a compounder I want to hold through raises - but a 10% stop, because at this multiple the downside if the talc settlement or STELARA erosion disappoints is real.

Held at 5% as the one staple that survives this week's cut, and the distinction from PEP is deliberate rather than sentimental. Coca-Cola is a dividend king with 60+ years of increases and, unlike its peer, it is still compounding on the tape: +11.5% over three months, +15.8% over six and +32.7% over twelve, only 4.3% below its high, against PEP at -11.8% over six months and 16.8% below its high. Its concentrate model is asset-light with genuine pricing power, which is the property I want if the jobs beat and $90s crude mean inflation is stickier than the market assumed. I keep the leg small at 5% because a 2.9% yield staple is still partly a bond substitute with the 10-year at 4.78%, and that caps how much I want. Tight 8% stop given that vulnerability; take-profit widened from an over-tight 6% to 12%.

New 5% position and the explicit hedge against the thing that broke my old book this week. Every other leg here would prefer lower rates; U.S. Bancorp is the one dividend grower that is better off if the blowout jobs report really does mean higher-for-longer or a hike, because higher-for-longer widens net interest margin on a deposit franchise that is 60%+ funded by low-cost core deposits. It qualifies on the mandate without a stretch - roughly 14 years of consecutive increases and a 3.27% forward yield - and it is the cheapest thing I own at 11.0x forward, with sell-side work this week arguing it is materially undervalued on the Sun Belt business-banking expansion. It is also quietly trending, +14.8% on the quarter and +23.3% over six months. Deliberately small at 5%: banks carry credit risk that staples and pharma do not, and if the 'blowout' payroll print is revised away - the same Yahoo analysis this week flagged the beat as less impressive than the headline - the rate tailwind reverses. 12% stop, 20% take-profit.

New 4% position - the smallest equity leg, and small on purpose. The attraction is real: 18.1x forward for a ~3.3% yield, 14 straight years of increases with a raise cadence in the high single digits, EPS guidance raised to $22.30-23.50, and the strongest three-month move in my healthcare sleeve at +25.8%. Repatha's data this week showing mortality reduction before a first cardiovascular event expands a franchise that is already the cash engine, and MariTide gives me free optionality on oral/convenient obesity dosing without paying an obesity multiple. The reason for 4% rather than 8% is a specific risk I found while checking it: Novartis's pelacarsen failed to reduce cardiovascular events in late-stage testing on Thursday, dragging AMGN down after hours in sympathy, and that failure is a genuine read-through to Amgen's own Lp(a) program. That is an unresolved binary I do not want size in. 12% stop to accommodate 27% vol, 20% take-profit.

New 3% position, the smallest in the book, added specifically as an inflation-linked income sleeve rather than an energy-price bet. Enterprise Products has raised its distribution for roughly 27 consecutive years - a longer unbroken growth streak than most of the aristocrats I own - at a yield near 6.5%, and its contracts carry fee escalators tied to PPI, so the cash flow literally indexes to the inflation that the $90s crude and the payroll beat are putting back on the table. Critically it is fee-based and volume-driven, not commodity-price-driven, so it diversifies the CVX leg instead of doubling it: 18.5% realised vol against CVX's 25.4%, +6.7% over six months and only 1.1% off its 52-week high, with distribution coverage comfortably above 1.5x. Kept to 3% because it is a midstream partnership rather than a corporate dividend payer and sits at the edge of the mandate. 10% stop, no take-profit - this leg is owned for the distribution, and selling it on a 10% price move would defeat the point.
